events.title: Samuel Hale tightens the herring barrels
events.body: The human cooper Samuel Hale takes down the leaking herring barrels of Baile dhìreach stave by stave and makes every one of them tight by the end of summer, beginning with the idle row of the salter Ruairidh. He takes a bowl from the pot for his pay, and asks for Dia-thìris words, which he writes under his own.

events.title: The first boat off the humans' slip
events.body: On the first evening of Lùnastal the humans' slip at Baile dhìreach launches a small coaster of the strangers' pattern, deeper in the keel than the boats of the south-west. She is built for the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim, paid for in fish and labour and rigged with the town's rope; his wife pours sea water on her bow and asks Manannan to keep her.

events.title: A stranger's prayer at the lamps of the drowned
events.body: At the dark of the year Baile dhìreach sets lamps along its quay for its drowned, as the harbours of the west do. The humans of the shingle stand in the line, and the cooper Samuel Hale says a prayer to Crìosd in his own tongue for shipmates lost in the northern sea on the voyage out. Eilidh nic Ruairidh sets a lamp for them.

events.title: The storm of the wolf-moon at Baile dhìreach
events.body: A three-day storm off the west drives the sea over the quay of Baile dhìreach and up the shingle towards the boats. On the second night the town and the humans haul the boats over the crest together with ropes, blocks and a capstan-bar from the slip. The salt-house chimney and half the roof of the humans' house are lost.

events.title: Pike writes of the natives
events.body: Thomas Pike enters in the post's letter-book that the islanders have agreed to the lights without difficulty and without asking what they would cost. It is the first page of his letter-book to call the Dia-thìrich the natives. The custodians' roll sets down the same asking as a request that the old sea-fires be built higher and kept all night.

events.title: The households of Àth dhearg asked hearth by hearth
events.body: The custodian of Àth dhearg will not give away the fire-shelf above the rock-cut stair, saying it belongs to the households who cut it. Torcall Clachair and James Fenn go round the hearths for eleven days. Most say yes and two say no. The third cairn is raised at the end of the shelf, and the custodian climbs up with bread.

events.title: No fire on Binnean a' Chlachair
events.body: James Fenn asks for a night fire on the summit of Binnean a' Chlachair, the highest ground of the island. Torcall Clachair and the herders of Muileann gheal refuse, keeping the custom of the hills. Torcall lays one stone on the herders' cairn, and Fenn takes his sights by day to a linen square, four days slower. The two winter at Muileann gheal.

events.title: Torcall witnesses in the Dia-thìreach book
events.body: At the wedding on the quay of Baile dhìreach no custodian comes to witness. James Fenn signs for the bridegroom in the humans' book, and Iain mac Chaluim calls the mason Torcall Clachair from the crowd to sign the Dia-thìreach book. William Rook and Iain mac Chaluim close the two books side by side.

events.title: Gormshuil called back from Muileann chaol
events.body: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, gone east with the season's copies for the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, is sent for by rider when the talks with Pell run fast. She starts back the day the rider finds her, but the rain is on the hills and the fords are up, and she is still on the road when the terms are signed.

events.title: Gormshuil given a copy of the terms
events.body: Two days after the signing Gormshuil nic Fhearchair comes in from the hills, reads the entry in the roll standing, and asks Pell through Samuel Wren for the terms in the strangers' tongue, since the copy in Dia-thìris is to wait for leisure. Pell's secretary makes one within the week. She begins to read it a word at a time, and does not bring it before the council.

events.title: The masons of the capital build for Pell
events.body: The masons of the masons' lane at Cathair dhearg take up Pell's house on the rise, paid in bar-iron by the humans' day, which begins at midnight where the island's begins at dusk. They float grey stone over the lake on rafts and build the house square to Pell's drawn plan, facing the harbour, with its back to the capital. The council does not ask it turned.

events.title: The warehouse door hung
events.body: The oak door of A' Chompanaidh's warehouse at Cathair dhomhain comes down the shore road from Cathair dhearg and is hung at dusk on strap hinges forged by Gilleasbuig Gobha in the smiths' lane below the bridge. Thomas Pike locks it with a long iron key. Tormod mac Ailein, who has walked out from the capital, watches it hung; the lake-shore roll calls it a good door.

events.title: The hill's coal carried to Cuan shean
events.body: Eleven carriers of the hills bring the measured coal for the western hearths down from the store at Taigh na Fèithe to Cuan shean, five days on the road with ponies and a custodian's clerk. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom goes among them for the first time. Oighrig nic Leòid counts the baskets in by lamplight at the custodians' store.

events.title: Six sacks come back to Muileann chrom
events.body: At the summer's end a human carter brings six of the thirteen sacks back up the road to the mill of Muileann chrom with a paper no one there can read. Asked for the rest, he points west, towards Ros dhomhain and the ships, and turns his cart round.

events.title: The first contract read at the mill
events.body: Abel Stone brings the first contract of A' Chompanaidh to Muileann chrom with two carts of steel-pointed picks, bar-iron and lamp-oil. It is read at the mill in both tongues. The interpreter from Ros dhomhain can find no Dia-thìris for the ton and calls it "a great load, weighed". Some of the older hewers walk out before the end.

events.title: Raghnall chosen to lead the thirty
events.body: Abel Stone names Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, who walked the seam with him, to lead the first crew of the hill. The crew is thirty: young men of the hewers' and shepherds' households, two from the mill and three older hewers of the old cutting. Raghnall's father, a hewer of that cutting, will not join it.
